To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) deaf adults with little or no accessible linguistic experience during early childhood perform poorly on all tasks of second language acquisition; and (b) deaf and hearing adults, regardless of sensory-motor form (hearing, spoken; deaf, signed) of the language they experienced during early childhood, perform well on second language acquisition.

the age at which language acquisition begins is a critical variable that affects the outcome of language acquisition throughout life and that this variable is independent of whether the early language experience is spoken or signed.

(i) the age of acquisition of a first language (L1) has a dramatic effect on the outcome of subsequent language acquisition, regardless of the form of the L2 (spoken or signed); and (ii) the outcome of L2 acquisition is related to the age of acquisition but not the form of the language (spoken or signed).
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the age of acquisition of a language affects its subsequent acquisition and the extent to which the sensory-motor modality of the first language experience affects this outcome.
the effects of early versus later exposure to a language, regardless of the sensory-motorsystem used to convey that language.
the question of whether there are age-related constraints on learning a language, regardless of the sensory-motorsystem involved.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the age of first language acquisition has a profound and permanent effect on the capacity of the human brain to acquire language, but that the effect is independent of the modality of the language experience.
the age of onset of language learning is the most important factor in determining ultimate success in language learning.
the age of first language acquisition is critical for the outcome of second language acquisition, but that the age of second language acquisition is not critical for the outcome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
early language experience is a necessary and sufficient factor for the acquisition of language.
the age of onset of language acquisition is a key variable in language acquisition, but not a sufficient condition.
the onset of accessible language experience in early human life alters the capacity to acquire language throughout life, regardless of sensory-motor modality of the early experience.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the critical period for language acquisition is not a single period of time but rather a series of periods, each of which is defined by a different aspect of language acquisition.
early language learning has a dramatic impact on the capacity for language learning later in life.
the onset of linguistic experience in early life has a profound effect on language learning throughout the lifespan, independent of whether the language experience was spoken or signed.
